questions.q: Why does a strong platform design write-up include a dedicated tradeoffs section instead of only listing proposed components?
options: Because tradeoffs sections are required by regulatory standards
Because naming the real costs and risks of a design, not just its benefits, is what makes the write-up credible to a reviewer
Because it makes the document longer, which is always preferred
Because proposed architecture sections are optional without it
questions.explain: A design with zero acknowledged downsides reads as either inexperienced or dishonest — the tradeoffs section is what signals the author actually understands the costs of their own proposal.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'vocabulary' and 'specificity' in a design write-up, as this lesson describes it?
options: There is no meaningful difference
Vocabulary names a component (e.g. 'a feature store'); specificity explains why it's needed and how it behaves (e.g. its online/offline latency split)
Specificity means using more technical jargon than necessary
Vocabulary only applies to code samples, specificity only applies to diagrams
questions.explain: Reviewers look for specificity — explaining why a component exists and how it functions in context — rather than just correctly naming the component.

questions.q: In this course's recap, what does Chapter 5 (Model Deployment Infrastructure) contribute to the Northline design from the capstone?

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is this course's position in the broader AI Infrastructure / ML Systems Engineer path?

It is the third course in the path, building on Distributed Training Infrastructure and assuming training is already solved
